steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on federated linear contextual bandits with heterogeneous clients. It should explain why the homogeneity assumption in existing federated bandit work is a problem, how collaborative and clustered bandits relate to this, what makes clustering hard under the federated communication protocol, and briefly present our two-stage algorithm and what we show about it.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
1. Bandit learning and the rise of federated bandit learning
2. The homogeneity assumption in existing federated bandits and why it fails
3. Collaborative / clustered bandits and their centralized setting
4. Our approach: federated bandits for heterogeneous clients, and the key challenges
5. The two-stage federated clustered bandit algorithm and our contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Bandit learning -> federated bandits
- bandit algorithms = reference solution for online decision optimization
- applications: recommender systems, clinical trials, display advertising
- usually run by centralized server; growing data from distributed systems -> demand for private, efficient, decentralized bandit learning across clients
- federated bandit learning: multiple clients collaborate to minimize cumulative regret, coordinated by single central server
- server only facilitates joint model estimation; no access to clients' arm pulling or reward history

2. Homogeneity assumption
- most existing approaches: all clients share same underlying bandit model -> near-optimal sub-linear regret for the population
- reduces federated bandits to joint estimation of single global model under federated learning communication protocol
- reality: diverse objectives -> different optimal policies
- single global model on heterogeneous clients -> can cost every client linear regret
- rational clients won't participate: can't tell beforehand if others share their model; already get sub-linear regret alone (worse than truly shared case)
- impedes practical application

3. Collaborative bandits
- improve bandit learning in heterogeneous environments via collective model estimation among clients
- clustered bandits: group similar clients, shared model within group
- relatedness given (e.g. affinity graph) -> joint policy learning analytically
- but mostly centralized: server has direct access to all clients' data
- can't address privacy + communication efficiency demands; significant effort to adapt to distributed settings

4. Our approach + challenges
- federated bandit learning among heterogeneous clients; extends collaborative bandits to standard federated setting
- goal: every participant gets regret reduction vs independent learning -> motivates participation
- first work of this kind: linear contextual bandit model per client (most common model in federated bandits)
- regret reduction via clustering clients, collective estimation only within cluster
- challenges in communication protocol: (1) no real-time access to client data -> delayed cluster inference; (2) server estimates/broadcasts one global model at a time -> congestion, delayed updates; both cost regret

5. Algorithm + contributions
- two-stage federated clustered bandit algorithm
- stage 1: pure exploration, non-parametric clustering via statistical homogeneity test
- stage 2: FIFO queue on server for event-triggered communication at cluster level
- upper bounds on cumulative regret and communication cost
- empirical enhancement: dynamic re-clustering in stage 2 + priority queue to improve regret
- comprehensive empirical comparison vs representative baselines

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Bandit learning algorithms are now a reference solution for problems of online decision optimization, and they are used in a lot of applications like recommender systems, clinical trials, and display advertising. Usually these algorithms are run by a centralized server. But because more and more data is being generated from distributed systems, there is a growing demand for bandit learning that is private, efficient and decentralized across multiple clients. Federated bandit learning has come up as a promising solution framework for this, where multiple clients work together to minimize their cumulative regret and a single central server coordinates them. The server only helps with joint model estimation across clients, and it does not have access to any client's arm pulling or reward history.

Federated bandit learning is getting more and more interest from the research community, but most existing approaches need all clients to share the same underlying bandit model so that near-optimal sub-linear regret can be achieved for a population of clients. With this strong homogeneity assumption, federated bandit learning basically becomes joint estimation of one single global model across clients, under the federated learning communication protocol. In reality, though, clients can have diverse objectives, and so they have different optimal policies. Imposing one global model on a heterogeneous population of clients can easily cost every client linear regret. So rational clients should choose not to participate in this kind of federated learning system, since they cannot know beforehand whether the other participating clients share the same bandit model with them, and they can already get sub-linear regret on their own (even though it is worse than the regret they would get if all clients really shared the same bandit model). This is a serious problem for the practical application of the existing federated bandit learning solutions.

There is also a parallel line of bandit research on collaborative bandits, which tries to improve bandit learning in heterogeneous environments by letting different clients do collective model estimation. For example, clustered bandit algorithms group similar clients together and use a shared bandit model for the clients that are in the same group. When the relatedness among clients is provided, for example through an affinity graph, joint policy learning can be done analytically. But most of the existing collaborative bandit learning algorithms work in a centralized setting, where it is assumed that data from all clients can be directly accessed by a central server. Because of this, these methods cannot address the demand for privacy and communication efficiency in online learning for distributed systems. A lot of effort is needed to adapt these algorithms to distributed settings.

4. Our approach + challenges
- federated bandit learning among heterogeneous clients; extends collaborative bandits to standard federated setting
- goal: every participant gets regret reduction vs independent learning -> motivates participation
- first work of this kind: linear contextual bandit model per client (most common model in federated bandits)
- regret reduction via clustering clients, collective estimation only within cluster
- challenges: (1) no real-time access to client data -> delayed cluster inference; (2) server estimates/broadcasts one global model at a time -> congestion, delayed updates; both cost regret

5. Algorithm + contributions
- two-stage federated clustered bandit algorithm
- stage 1: pure exploration, non-parametric clustering via statistical homogeneity test
- stage 2: FIFO queue on server for event-triggered communication at cluster level
- upper bounds on cumulative regret and communication cost
- empirical enhancement: dynamic re-clustering in stage 2 + priority queue
- comprehensive empirical comparison vs representative baselines

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Bandit learning algorithms are now a reference solution for problems of online decision optimization, and they are used in a lot of applications like recommender systems, clinical trials, and display advertising. Usually these algorithms are run by a centralized server. But because more and more data is being generated from distributed systems, there is a growing demand for bandit learning that is private, efficient and decentralized across multiple clients. Federated bandit learning has come up as a promising solution framework for this, where multiple clients work together to minimize their cumulative regret and a single central server coordinates them. The server only helps with joint model estimation across clients, and it does not have access to any client's arm pulling or reward history.

Federated bandit learning is getting more and more interest from the research community, but most existing approaches need all clients to share the same underlying bandit model so that near-optimal sub-linear regret can be achieved for a population of clients. With this strong homogeneity assumption, federated bandit learning basically becomes joint estimation of one single global model across clients, under the federated learning communication protocol. In reality, though, clients can have diverse objectives, and so they have different optimal policies. Imposing one global model on a heterogeneous population of clients can easily cost every client linear regret. So rational clients should choose not to participate in this kind of federated learning system, since they cannot know beforehand whether the other participating clients share the same bandit model with them, and they can already get sub-linear regret on their own (even though it is worse than the regret they would get if all clients really shared the same bandit model). This is a serious problem for the practical application of the existing federated bandit learning solutions.

There is also a parallel line of bandit research on collaborative bandits, which tries to improve bandit learning in heterogeneous environments by letting different clients do collective model estimation. For example, clustered bandit algorithms group similar clients together and use a shared bandit model for the clients that are in the same group. When the relatedness among clients is provided, for example through an affinity graph, joint policy learning can be done analytically. But most of the existing collaborative bandit learning algorithms work in a centralized setting, where it is assumed that data from all clients can be directly accessed by a central server. Because of this, these methods cannot address the demand for privacy and communication efficiency in online learning for distributed systems. A lot of effort is needed to adapt these algorithms to distributed settings.

In this paper we introduce a new approach for federated bandit learning among heterogeneous clients, which extends collaborative bandit learning to the standard federated learning setting. The goal is to make sure every participating client gets a regret reduction compared to learning independently, so that all clients are motivated to participate. Because this is the first work of this kind, we focus on estimating a linear contextual bandit model for each client, which is also the model most commonly used in federated bandits. It is not surprising that regret reduction in a population of heterogeneous clients can be achieved by clustering the clients and doing collective model estimation only inside each cluster. The key challenges are in the communication protocol of federated learning. First, the server does not have real-time access to the data of each client, so its inferences of the client clusters are delayed. Second, the server can only estimate and broadcast one global model at a time. This can cause communication congestion and delay the model updates. Both of these things cost regret.

To deal with these challenges we develop a two-stage federated clustered bandit algorithm. In the first stage, all clients do pure exploration so that a non-parametric clustering of the clients can be prepared, based on the statistical homogeneity test. Then in the second stage, the server keeps a first-in-first-out queue to make event-triggered communication possible at the cluster level. We rigorously prove upper bounds of the cumulative regret and the communication cost for this algorithm. After that, we improve the algorithm empirically by allowing clients to be re-clustered dynamically in the second stage and by using a priority queue to improve regret. We also run comprehensive empirical comparisons of the new federated bandit algorithm against a set of representative baselines to show that our proposed framework is effective.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Bandit learning algorithms [1,2,3,4] have become a reference solution to problems of online decision optimization in a wide variety of applications, including recommender systems [3], clinical trials [5], and display advertising [6]. Typically these algorithms are operated by a centralized server; but because of the growing quantity of data generated from distributed systems, there is a surge in demand for private, efficient, and decentralized bandit learning across multiple clients. Federated bandit learning has emerged as a promising solution framework, in which multiple clients collaborate to minimize their cumulative regret under the coordination of a single central server [7,8,9,10,11]. The server's role is limited to facilitating joint model estimation across clients, and it has no access to any client's arm pulling or reward history.

Although federated bandit learning has gained increasing interest from the research community, most existing approaches require that all clients share the same underlying bandit model in order to achieve near-optimal sub-linear regret for a population of clients. This strong homogeneity assumption reduces federated bandit learning to a joint estimation of a single global model across clients, subject to the federated learning communication protocol [12,13]. In reality, however, clients can have diverse objectives, which result in different optimal policies. Imposing a single global model on a heterogeneous client population can easily cost every client linear regret [14]. Consequently, rational clients should choose not to participate in such a federated learning system, as they cannot determine beforehand whether other participating clients share the same bandit model with them, and they can already achieve sub-linear regret independently (albeit inferior to the regret obtained when all clients genuinely share the same bandit model). This seriously impedes the practical application of existing federated bandit learning solutions.

In a parallel line of bandit research, studies in collaborative bandits aim to improve bandit learning in heterogeneous environments by facilitating collective model estimation among different clients. For example, clustered bandit algorithms group similar clients and use a shared bandit model for clients within the same group [15,16,17,18,19]. When the relatedness among clients is provided, such as through an affinity graph, joint policy learning can be performed analytically [18,19]. However, most existing collaborative bandit learning algorithms operate under a centralized setting, in which data from all clients is assumed to be directly accessible by a central server. As a result, these methods cannot address the demand for privacy and communication efficiency in online learning for distributed systems, and significant efforts are required to adapt them to distributed settings [20].

In this paper, we introduce a novel approach for federated bandit learning among heterogeneous clients, which extends collaborative bandit learning to the standard federated learning setting. The goal is to ensure that every participating client achieves regret reduction compared to independent learning, thereby motivating all clients to participate. As the first work of this kind, we focus on estimating a linear contextual bandit model [3,4] for each client, which is also the most commonly employed model in federated bandits. Not surprisingly, regret reduction in a population of heterogeneous clients can be realized by clustering the clients and performing collective model estimation only within each cluster. The key challenges, however, lie in the communication protocol of federated learning. First, the server lacks real-time access to each client's data, which delays its inferences of client clusters. Second, the server can only estimate and broadcast one global model at a time [21,22], which can cause communication congestion and delay model updates. Both cost regret.

To address these challenges, we develop a two-stage federated clustered bandit algorithm. In the first stage, all clients perform pure exploration to prepare a non-parametric clustering of clients based on the statistical homogeneity test [23]. In the second stage, a first-in-first-out queue is maintained on the server side to facilitate event-triggered communication [7] at the cluster level. We rigorously establish upper bounds on the cumulative regret and communication cost of this algorithm. We then empirically enhance the algorithm by allowing dynamic re-clustering of clients in the second stage and by employing a priority queue to improve regret. Finally, we conduct comprehensive empirical comparisons of the newly proposed federated bandit algorithm against a set of representative baselines to demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework.
